Weighted sampling

Source: R/design-weighted.R
design_weighted.Rd

Draws rows with probability governed by a weights column. The weights are used as supplied: prob= normalises by their sum, so rescaling them changes nothing and the design does not offer it.

Usage

design_weighted(
  weights,
  n,
  replace = FALSE,
  method = c("successive", "systematic", "poisson"),
  na_rm = FALSE,
  strata = NULL,
  allocation = c("proportional", "equal")
)

Arguments

weights

Column of positive, finite, numeric weights. A weight of 0 is refused under every method, not given a probability of 0; drop such rows from the frame first, since a design that selects in proportion to size could never select them.

n

Number of rows to draw, the total across strata when given, or a plan from plan_size(). Under method = "poisson" this is the expected number, not a guarantee. With counts in allocation it can be left out and is their sum; when given, it must equal that sum.

replace

Sample with replacement? Only available for method = "successive".

method

One of "successive", "systematic" or "poisson". See "Choosing a method".

na_rm

Drop rows whose weight or stratum key is NA instead of raising an error.

strata

Optional column name(s) defining strata, to sample in proportion to size within each one. Several columns are cross-classified. Needs method = "systematic" or "poisson". See "Strata".

allocation

How n is split across strata: "proportional" to the number of rows in each stratum, or "equal", by the largest-remainder method of design_stratified(), with a stratum that would get more rows than it holds taken whole; or the count for each stratum, as a named vector such as c(north = 10, south = 5) when strata is one column, or a data frame of the strata columns and n. Counts follow the rules of design_stratified(): every stratum of the frame needs one, a count for a stratum the frame does not have is refused, and no count may exceed the rows in its stratum. Only with strata.

Value

A design object, for use with draw().

Choosing a method

The three methods differ in what the weights actually control, which decides whether the sample can be used for estimation.

"successive"

The default, and what base::sample() does. The weights govern each sequential draw, not the probability that a row ends up in the sample, and the realised inclusion probabilities are not proportional to the weights. How far off depends on the weights: with a single dominant unit the two nearly coincide (about 1% apart), but with a moderate spread the gap is large — weights 1:10 at n = 5 give inclusion probabilities up to about 36% away from proportional, by exact enumeration of the ordered draws. Treating them as if they were proportional biases a Horvitz-Thompson total by around 1% at n = 15 out of 30 in simulation, small in size but unmistakable in sign. There is no closed form for pi, so inclusion_prob() refuses to give one. Fine when you want a weighted selection; wrong as the basis for an estimate.

"systematic"

Randomised systematic probability-proportional-to- size (Madow 1949; Hartley and Rao 1962). Shuffles the rows, then walks the cumulative weights with a fixed step from a random start, giving pi_i = n * p_i exactly. Rows heavy enough that n * p_i > 1 are taken with certainty and the rest rescaled, repeatedly, until every probability is valid. Fixed sample size. The shuffle means every pair of rows can appear together, but their joint probabilities have no closed form, so ht_total() uses Deville's approximation for the variance, which needs only the first-order probabilities.

"poisson"

Each row is included independently with probability pi_i = n * p_i. Rows heavy enough that n * p_i > 1 are taken with certainty and the rest rescaled, repeatedly, as for "systematic", so the probabilities still sum to n. Inclusion probabilities are exactly proportional to size among the rows below certainty, and every pair can co-occur, at the cost of a random sample size averaging n.

replace = TRUE is with-replacement PPS and applies only to method = "successive".

Strata

With strata, n is split over the strata by allocation, as design_stratified() splits it over the rows in each stratum, and each stratum is then sampled in proportion to size on its own: a row of stratum h gets n_h * w_i / sum(w), the sum running over the stratum, with rows past certainty taken with certainty within it. Under "systematic" each stratum is shuffled and walked from a start of its own, in key order; under "poisson" every row is included independently with the probability its stratum gives it, so the size of each stratum's sample is random. "successive" has no closed-form inclusion probability and is refused with strata. To split n in proportion to each stratum's total size rather than its rows, work out the counts and give them as allocation.

The strata are sampled independently. ht_total() and ht_mean() add up Deville's approximation over the strata for "systematic", and the Poisson variance needs no change. The degrees of freedom are the sampled rows below certainty less the strata that hold them. A stratum with one sampled row below certainty has nothing to compare it with, and the variance is refused with the stratum named; draw at least two in each.

In simulations of 2,000 draws each from frames of 600 rows in four strata, drawing 24 or 60 rows by "systematic", the variance averaged 0.94 to 1.04 times the true variance of the total, and 95% intervals covered 89% to 96% of the time. The low coverage came where y / pi was skewed, so that samples with a low total also had a low estimated variance; the same frames without strata covered 92% to 94%.

as_svydesign() hands the strata to survey, with Brewer's approximation within each, allocation_table() shows the split before anything is drawn, and sample_summary() counts the rows drawn from each stratum.

Drawing each stratum with a design of its own and binding the samples with rbind() does not give a sample to estimate from. The bound sample keeps the first draw's frame and design, so ht_total() refuses it; use strata instead.

References

Madow, W. G. (1949). On the theory of systematic sampling, II. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 20, 333–354. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177729988

Hartley, H. O. and Rao, J. N. K. (1962). Sampling with unequal probabilities and without replacement. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 33, 350–374. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177704564

Brewer, K. R. W. and Hanif, M. (1983). Sampling with Unequal Probabilities. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4684-9407-5

Tillé, Y. (2006). Sampling Algorithms. Springer. doi:10.1007/0-387-34240-0

See also

draw(), inclusion_prob(), certainty_set() for the rows taken with certainty, design_spread() to select in proportion to size and spread the sample across a map. The sampling package implements further fixed-size unequal-probability algorithms (Brewer, Sampford, Tillé, maximum entropy) as vector functions.

Other designs: design_bootstrap(), design_certainty(), design_cluster(), design_multistage(), design_reservoir(), design_simple(), design_spatial(), design_spread(), design_stratified(), design_systematic(), design_temporal()

Examples

df <- data.frame(id = 1:20, w = 1:20)
draw(df, design_weighted("w", n = 5), seed = 1)
#>   id  w
#> 1 18 18
#> 2 16 16
#> 3 12 12
#> 4  6  6
#> 5 19 19

# Inclusion probabilities proportional to size, and checkable
d <- design_weighted("w", n = 5, method = "systematic")
round(inclusion_prob(df, d), 3)
#>  [1] 0.024 0.048 0.071 0.095 0.119 0.143 0.167 0.190 0.214 0.238 0.262 0.286
#> [13] 0.310 0.333 0.357 0.381 0.405 0.429 0.452 0.476

# Which is what makes an unbiased total possible
s <- draw(df, d, seed = 1, weights = TRUE)
sum(s$w * s$.weight)   # estimates sum(df$w) = 210
#> [1] 210

# In proportion to size within each of two regions
df$region <- rep(c("east", "west"), each = 10)
by_region <- design_weighted("w", n = 8, method = "systematic",
                             strata = "region")
allocation_table(df, by_region)
#>   region  N n prob sd cost status
#> 1   east 10 4   NA NA   NA   rule
#> 2   west 10 4   NA NA   NA   rule
round(inclusion_prob(df, by_region), 3)
#>  [1] 0.073 0.145 0.218 0.291 0.364 0.436 0.509 0.582 0.655 0.727 0.284 0.310
#> [13] 0.335 0.361 0.387 0.413 0.439 0.465 0.490 0.516
